sentences.text: This woman is about to win, and she has it completely wrong.
This is Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses, painted by John William Waterhouse in 1891.
Everyone sees Circe, the witch of the Odyssey, trapping another man.
She has already turned his crew into pigs.
And the picture seems to agree.
She raises her wand and holds out the cup like a queen.
According to the Odyssey, Hermes warned him and showed him a plant that made him immune to her potion.
She touches him with the wand, sure the potion has worked.
Then he draws his sword, and she must give his sailors back.
She's the one walking into a trap.
So who is really caught, the hero, or the woman with the cup?

meta.title: She Offered Him the Cup... But He Was Already IMMUNE #history #art
meta.description: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses was painted by John William Waterhouse in 1891 and hangs in Gallery Oldham. Ulysses is visible in the mirror behind her; in the Odyssey, Hermes had already given him a plant that made him immune to her potion.
meta.question: Who is really caught?

sources.claim: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses is an oil painting in the Pre-Raphaelite style by John William Waterhouse that was created in 1891.
Circe, a sorceress, offers a cup to Odysseus (commonly Ulysses in English).
Two of Ulysses' crewmen have been transformed into pigs; one can be seen beside Circe's feet on the right, while the other is peering out from behind her throne on the left.
Ulysses' reflection can be seen in the mirror behind Circe's throne, in addition to the columns of her palace and Ulysses' ship.
He advises Ulysses to find a special plant that makes him immune to the effects of Circe's potion, which he proceeds to do.
Under the impression that the effects of the potion have taken hold, Circe touches Ulysses with her wand to complete the transformation process.
He reluctantly agrees, and, after the arrangement is consummated, she returns his sailors to their human form.
